1.01.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this implant made of?"
- "Trauma implants are **stainless steel** or **titanium**."
- "Joints add cobalt-chrome, ceramic and polyethylene."

| Material | Tell it by | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| **316L stainless steel** | smooth polished surface | plates, screws, nails, pins |
| **Titanium alloy** | matt, micro-rough surface | plates, screws, uncemented stems |
| **Cobalt-chrome** | stiffest metal, low wear | femoral heads, cemented stems |
| **Tantalum** | very porous metal | acetabular reconstruction, revision cups |
| **Ceramic** | hardest, brittle | bearing surfaces only |
| **Polyethylene (PE)** | white plastic | cup liners, tibial inserts |
| **PEEK, absorbable** | radiolucent plastic | cages, anchors, small pins |

- Ceramics and polymers never carry high loads alone
- Cost: steel is cheapest, cobalt-chrome dearest

- Steel stems, cobalt-chrome head, titanium stems

### What every implant material needs
- Non-toxic, with no harmful tissue reaction
- High yield strength and high fatigue resistance
- Resistant to wear and corrosion, and affordable (Handbook)

#### Three generations
| Generation | Behaviour | Example |
|---|---|---|
| First | bioinert | metal implants |
| Second | bioactive or degradable | absorbable screws |
| Third | bioactive and degradable | HA-coated polymers |

#### Biocompatibility
- The material performs with the right host response
- In that use and in that place

### Stainless steel (316L)
- Iron with chromium, nickel and molybdenum
- "L" means low carbon: better corrosion resistance
- Chromium makes the protective oxide layer

#### Why surgeons like it
- Ductile: you can bend a plate to fit the bone
- It warns you before the screw head breaks
- Kinder under tendons: they glide freely over polished steel

| Distal radius model (AO) | Tendon glide |
|---|---|
| Polished steel | **100%** |
| Non-polished titanium | **43%** |

#### Its problems
- Crevice corrosion
- Implant steel holds **13–16%** nickel
- Nickel allergy in **1–2%**: use titanium

### Titanium
- Commercially pure titanium, or alloys such as titanium–aluminium–niobium (TAN)
- About **10%** weaker than steel; a thicker implant makes up for it
- Better fatigue life under repeated load

#### Its problems
- Low ductility gives little warning
- Bone grows onto it: hard to remove
- Poor wear, notch sensitive: never a bearing surface

#### Tightening a screw (AO)
| Metal | After maximum torque | Torque |
|---|---|---|
| Steel | about **1.5** more turns, then breaks | peaks first |
| Titanium | **3–4** more turns | keeps rising |

- Use a torque-limiting screwdriver

#### Its bonuses
- Almost no corrosion and no proven allergy
- Non-magnetic: fewer MRI artefacts

- Titanium plate, ceramic head and titanium stems

### Cobalt-chrome, tantalum, ceramic
| Material | Key fact | So |
|---|---|---|
| **Cobalt-chrome** | highest modulus of the metals | femoral heads, cemented stems |
| **Tantalum** | very porous, low modulus | bone grows into it |
| **Ceramic** | stiffest and hardest | bearings, never a stem |

- Cobalt-chrome is not used in fracture plates: galvanic corrosion with steel
- Ceramic is strong in compression, poor in bending
- Ceramic revision → ch 10

- Ceramic femoral heads through four generations
- Porous tantalum implant

### Plastics
- **UHMWPE** = ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene
- Cross-linking cuts its wear by up to **90%**
- Metal-on-polyethylene is still the gold-standard bearing (Prof Mahmoud Fahmy)

#### Bone cement, PEEK, absorbables
- Bone cement (PMMA) is a grout, not a glue → ch 10
- PEEK (polyetheretherketone): radiolucent, MRI compatible; for spine cages, suture anchors
- Absorbable polylactides: low loads only, as small pins and anchors

#### Coatings
- Hydroxyapatite (HA) coated pins bond to bone and cut pin-track infection
- But the coating can peel off the implant
- HA layers are **10–60 µm** thick (AO)

- Polyethylene acetabular liner
- PEEK cage and absorbable screws

### Which material for what
| Need | Choose |
|---|---|
| Plate to contour | stainless steel |
| Nickel allergy, MRI later | titanium |
| Cemented stem | cobalt-chrome or steel |
| Uncemented stem or cup | titanium |
| Bearing head | cobalt-chrome or ceramic |

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Steel bends, titanium flexes, cobalt wears well, ceramic shatters**

1.02.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "draw a stress–strain curve"
- "Stress on the vertical axis, strain on the horizontal."
- "Straight elastic part, yield point, plastic part, breaking point."
- "The **slope** of the straight part is Young's modulus."

### The two words
| Term | Means | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| **Stress** | force per area | pascal |
| **Strain** | change in length / original length | none |

### Reading the curve
- Elastic zone: remove the load, the shape comes back
- **Yield point**: elastic ends, permanent bending starts
- Plastic zone: the shape never comes back

#### Top of the curve
- **Ultimate strength** = highest stress on the curve
- Breaking point = where it snaps

#### Area under the curve
- **Toughness** = area under the curve
- **Resilience** = area under the elastic part only

- Stress–strain curve with its zones and points

### Stiffness = Young's modulus
- Steep slope = stiff; flat slope = flexible
- Implant stiffness = its material plus its shape and size
- Tibial nails: whole-system torsional rigidity matters more than the metal (AO)

| Young's modulus (AO) | GPa |
|---|---|
| Stainless steel | **186** |
| Titanium | **110** |
| Cortical bone | **20** |

- Order: ceramic, cobalt-chrome, steel, titanium, cortical bone, PMMA, PE, cancellous

- Young's modulus of orthopaedic materials, stiffest first

### Ductile, brittle, hard
- Ductile: long plastic zone, like steel
- Brittle: almost no plastic zone, like ceramic and glass
- Hardness: resists scratching; ceramic is the hardest

#### Notch sensitivity
- A scratch or crack starts the break, like a glass cutter's notch
- Titanium alloy is notch sensitive; ceramic too

- Brittle versus ductile material, and toughness
- Fractured ceramic femoral head

### Bone itself
- Viscoelastic: stiffer when loaded fast
- Anisotropic: strongest in compression, weakest in shear

| Cancellous vs cortical (Miller) | Cancellous has |
|---|---|
| Density | **25%** |
| Stiffness | **10%** |
| Ductility | **500%** |

### Fatigue and creep
- **Fatigue**: breaks under repeated loads below its ultimate strength
- Below the endurance limit it survives over **10⁶** cycles
- **Creep**: slow deformation under a constant load

### Corrosion — four types
| Type | Cause |
|---|---|
| **Galvanic** | two different metals touching |
| **Crevice** | cracks with low oxygen |
| **Fretting** | micromotion rubbing the surface |
| **Stress** | areas of high stress |

- Worst galvanic pair: 316L steel with cobalt-chrome
- Steel is the metal most prone to crevice corrosion

#### In practice
- Fretting: a screw head moving in its plate hole
- Prevent it: similar metals, good design, a passive oxide layer

- Galvanic, crevice and fretting corrosion
- Fretting and corrosion on a retrieved head and trunnion

PITFALL — "is a stiffer implant always better?"
- A stiff implant takes the load off the bone
- Say → "**No. Stiffness must suit the fracture; titanium is closer to bone.**"

1.03.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "stress shielding vs stress riser?"
- "Shielding: bone **loses density under** a stiff implant."
- "Riser: stress **piles up at** a hole or the plate end, and it breaks there."

### Two words that differ
- **Stability** belongs to the fracture: how little it moves
- **Rigidity** belongs to the implant: how little it bends
- There is no "rigid stability": only absolute or relative (Prof Abdel Karim)

| | Absolute | Relative |
|---|---|---|
| Motion | none under load | controlled |
| Made by | reduction plus compression | nail, bridge plate, fixator |
| Heals by | direct remodelling | callus |

- A fully locked plate works as an internal fixator: relative stability

### Strain decides the healing
- Strain = gap change / gap width

| Tissue tolerates (AO) | Strain |
|---|---|
| Granulation tissue | **100%** |
| Cartilage | **15%** |
| Cortical bone | **2%** |

#### Thresholds

| Strain (Miller) | Healing |
|---|---|
| Under **2%** | primary, no callus |
| **2–10%** | secondary, callus |
| Over **10%** | no bone forms |

#### Too little motion
- Too stiff a fixation, or too wide a gap → no callus
- Dynamisation lets the gap close and heal
- Perren strain theory and plates → ch 5

- Small gap versus large gap under the same motion
- Bridged simple fracture versus bridged comminuted fracture

### Working length
- Distance between the fixation points nearest the fracture
- Longer working length → less stiff construct
- Bending stiffness falls with its **square** (Handbook)

#### Bending and torsion
- Plates and fixators resist bending; nails resist bending and torsion

| Shape (Miller) | Bending rigidity rises with |
|---|---|
| Plate | thickness **cubed** |
| Nail, half-pin | radius to the **fourth** power |

### Stress shielding vs stress riser
| | Stress shielding | Stress riser |
|---|---|---|
| What | thin, porotic bone under the implant | fracture at a hole or plate end |
| Why | implant carries the load | stress concentrates at a defect |
| Where | under plates, femoral calcar | empty hole, last screw |

- A hole of **20–30%** of bone diameter cuts strength by up to half
- Bone at a removed screw hole recovers in **9–12** months

- Last plate screw, porosis and refracture in detail → ch 5

- Osteopenia under a long plate after healing
- Bone loss around an uncemented hip stem
- Fracture at the stress riser below a stiff stem

PITFALL — "porosis under a plate is pure stress shielding?"
- Perren showed early porosis follows the damaged blood supply
- Say → "**Mostly necrosis from plate contact, not unloading. Limited-contact plates reduce it.**"

1.04.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this clamp with two points?"
- "A **pointed reduction clamp (Weber)**: the first choice to reduce a fracture."
- "Its points hold bone gently, sparing the periosteum."

- Exam photos often show instruments on a green background (Handbook)

### Pointed reduction clamp (Weber)
- Each point sits on bone, directly or in a small drill hole
- Transverse fracture: one clamp on each main fragment, then pull

#### Oblique fracture
1) Tilt one clamp across both fragments
2) Rotate and squeeze to gain length
3) Swap to a second clamp at right angles to the fracture

- Pointed reduction clamp, and one reducing a Lisfranc joint
- Two-clamp technique, then one tilted clamp

### Holding the plate
| Clamp (AO) | Look for | Job |
|---|---|---|
| **Toothed reduction forceps** | serrated jaws | holds plate on forearm, fibula |
| **Verbrugge** | one end hooks round bone | centres plate on bone |
| **Bone spreader** | blades open outward | distracts to gain length |

- Verbrugge strips around the bone: use it outside the fracture zone

#### Push–pull with an independent screw
- Spreader between plate end and screw pushes the fracture out to length
- Small Verbrugge hooked on the same screw pulls it into compression

- Toothed forceps, Verbrugge forceps and bone spreader
- Push–pull: spreader to distract, Verbrugge to compress

### Big and pelvic clamps
- Three clamp families: bone-holding, plate-holding, reduction

| Clamp | Key feature |
|---|---|
| **Collinear** | sliding shaft, linear force, percutaneous |
| **King or Queen tong** | ball points stop deep penetration |
| **Matta** | angled; passes the sciatic notch |
| **Farabeuf** | grips screw heads; no distraction |
| **Jungbluth** | screwed to bone; moves in three planes |

- Collinear, ball-point and angled pelvic clamps
- Farabeuf and Jungbluth clamps

### Push and pull tools
- Ball-spike pusher: pushes a fragment into place
- Bone hook or dental pick: fine-tunes a small fragment

#### Lift and steer
- Bone impactor: lifts depressed joint fragments
- **Joystick**: a Schanz screw or K-wire steers a fragment

- Ball spike pushing and bone hook pulling a fracture

PITFALL — "toothed clamp for every reduction?"
- Toothed jaws slip and strip the periosteum
- Say → "**Pointed clamp first; it is gentle. Toothed clamps hold plates.**"

1.05.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this retractor with a narrow tip?"
- "A **Hohmann retractor**: its small curved tip goes round the bone to lever tissue away."

### Retractors
| Retractor (Handbook) | Look for |
|---|---|
| **Hohmann** | small, slightly curved tip on a broad blade |
| **Self-retaining (Gelpi)** | two blades hinged in the middle |
| **Langenbeck** | L-shaped blade |
| **Volkmann** | forked, like a rake |

- Open-fracture tray: Langenbeck, Sofield, Army-Navy retractors (Harborview)

- Hohmann retractors
- Hohmann retractors placed around the acetabulum
- Gelpi self-retaining retractor, and a self-retainer at the hip

### The Hohmann as a reduction tool
1) Slide the tip between the two cortices
2) Turn it **180°** to catch the opposite cortex
3) Lever gently; turn again to remove it

#### Safe and unsafe
- No extra stripping: the tip stays inside the fracture
- Unseen crack or osteoporosis: it can displace the fracture (AO)
- Hohmann lifting a sagging DHS → ch 6

- Small Hohmann used to reduce a shaft fracture

### Periosteal elevator
- Rounded, sloping blade: lifts the periosteum
- Cobb elevator: frees soft tissue off a plate at removal
- Freer elevator: lifts the plate end at removal (Harborview)

- Cobb elevator at the hip

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Hohmann hooks, self-retainer holds, Langenbeck lifts, Volkmann rakes**

1.06.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "osteotome or chisel?"
- "**Osteotome**: bevelled on both sides; it cuts straight through bone."
- "**Chisel**: bevelled on one side; it removes chips and layers."

| Instrument (Handbook) | Blade | Job |
|---|---|---|
| **Osteotome** | bevel both sides | cuts bone |
| **Chisel** | bevel one side | removes chips, layers |
| **Gouge** | curved, spoon-shaped | harvests cancellous graft |
| **Curette** | flat oval blade, no bevel | clears cavities |
| **Rasp** | serrated surface | smooths bone |

- Box osteotome: rectangular and hollow
- Mallet: the basic tool that drives them

- Osteotome, chisel and curettes; the bevels compared
- Osteotomes driven with a mallet

### Rongeur and cutters
- **Rongeur**: the correct name for the "bone nibbler"
- Kerrison rongeur: removes ligamentum flavum in spine surgery (Campbell)

| Cutter | Blade |
|---|---|
| **Pin cutter** | short |
| **Bone cutter** | longer, bird-beak |

- Fine rongeur

### Saws
- **Oscillating saw**: keep it constantly cooled
- Stop short of the far cortex; finish with drill holes or a chisel (AO)
- Olecranon chevron osteotomy: saw first, then lever it open with an osteotome

#### Gigli saw
- Passed round the bone on a heavy suture
- Smooth corticotomy, with no crack into pin sites (Campbell)

- Oscillating saw on a model, and an olecranon chevron cut
- Gigli saw shortening a femur

PITFALL — "can I cut the bone with a chisel?"
- The chisel's single bevel is made to remove layers
- Say → "**Osteotome to cut; chisel to remove chips.**"

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Two bevels cut, one bevel shaves, a spoon scoops**

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "drill or reamer?"
- "A **drill** makes a hole for a screw."
- "A **reamer** widens a canal or a socket."

### Basic tools on the tray
| Tool (Handbook) | Job |
|---|---|
| Drill bit | makes the hole |
| Depth gauge | measures screw length |
| Tap | cuts the thread |
| Screwdriver | drives the screw |
| Suction tip | clears the field |

### Drill
- Drill bit parts, tap and depth gauge → ch 4
- Heat necrosis and how to avoid it → ch 4
- Rule: sharp bit, drill sleeve, saline cooling

### Reamers
- Flexible reamers open and debride the medullary canal
- The reamer head can probe the canal diameter

#### Reaming hard bone
- Power reaming heats sclerotic bone: keep heads sharp and clean (AO)
- Reaming effects and nail size → ch 7

- Acetabular reamer widening the socket

PITFALL — "power tapping saves time?"
- Power tapping is not recommended (Nagah)
- Say → "**Tap by hand, through a sleeve.**"

1.08.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this set?"
- "An **implant removal set**: screwdrivers, extraction screws and hollow reamers."
- "It frees stripped or broken screws."

### Before you remove
- X-ray: union complete, implant type and position
- Have the right removal set in the room
- Leave implants at least **1–2** years first

#### Why remove
- Main indication: implant pain or soft-tissue irritation

#### Usually left in
- Elderly patients: removal risks refracture
- Forearm, humerus, pelvis: nerve and vessel risk (AO)
- External fixators and K-wires always come out

### Tools in the set
| Tool | Job |
|---|---|
| **Screwdriver, matching tip** | normal screw out |
| **Conical extraction screw** | reverse thread grips a damaged screw |
| **Hollow reamer (trephine)** | cores around a broken screw |
| **Extraction bolt, slide hammer** | pulls out a nail (Harborview) |

- The conical screw turns anticlockwise and backs the screw out
- Ingrown nail holes can be drilled out before extraction

- Conical extraction screw on a broken screw
- Stripped locking screws drilled free with an extractor

### Stripped locking screws
- Small locking screw heads strip most

| Locking screw (Park 2019) | Heads damaged at removal |
|---|---|
| 3.5 mm | **5.7–10.3%** |
| 5.0 mm | **0–0.7%** |

- Causes: wrong insertion angle, no torque limiter, worn screwdriver

#### Ways out
- Conical extraction screw
- Burr off the head, or cut the plate
- Hollow reamer: risks a large bone defect

### Freeing a plate
1) Expose the plate ends through small incisions
2) Free the plate edges with an elevator
3) Bone hook in the end hole, backslap with a mallet

- Bone hook in the end hole of a plate
- Plate backslapped out with a mallet

PITFALL — "titanium plate, same easy removal?"
- Bone grows onto titanium; locked screws can cold-weld
- Say → "**Plan it: full removal set, torque limiter, X-rays first.**"
